In the companion paper Abac et al. [4], we describe the significant transient GW candidates in GWTC-5.0, highlighting those observed in O4b. GWTC-5.0 also provides the inferred properties of the GW, as well as their sources, e.g., the masses and spins of the binary components under the assumption that the GW were produced by CBC. The exceptional O4b event papers on GW241011_233834 and GW241110_124123 [12], GW250114_082203 [13, 19], and GW240925_005809 and GW250207_115645 [20]. The GWTC dataset, along with other open data products, is detailed in the companion paper Abac et al. [9].

V.1.3 Gravitational Lensing of GW

Like electromagnetic waves, GW can be gravitationally lensed by massive objects, e.g., galaxies, interposed between the GW source and the observer. Because of the principle of equivalence, the GW polarization state is not affected by the gravitational interaction with a lensing non-rotating mass [232], so it is sufficient to consider scalar diffraction theory [296]. For rotating masses and in general for gravitomagnetic fields this requires corrections [262]. In a thin-lens approximation, the bending of the trajectory of the GW propagation occurs on a lens plane orthogonal to the line of sight and at the distance of the lensing body. With ξ1\xi_{1} and ξ2\xi_{2} as the coordinates of the lens plane, at each point on this plane there is an observed time delay T⁡(ξ1,ξ2)T(\xi_{1},\xi_{2}) relative to straight-line motion with no lens, corresponding to the path from the source to that point on the lens plane to the observer. This delay accounts for the gravitational field of the lens. GW are deflected by a gravitational lens with the time delay field on the lens plane determining the complex phases of the interfering partial waves used to compute a frequency-dependent complex-valued magnification factor. This factor is given by the Fresnel–Kirchhoff diffraction formula

F⁡(f)=i​DOSDOL​DLS​(1+zL)​fc​∬exp⁡[−2​π​i​f​T​(ξ1,ξ2)]​d​ξ1​d​ξ2,F(f)=i\frac{D_{\scriptscriptstyle\text{OS}}}{D_{\scriptscriptstyle\text{OL}}D_{\scriptscriptstyle\text{LS}}}\frac{(1+z_{\scriptscriptstyle\text{L}})f}{c}\iint\exp\left[-2\pi ifT(\xi_{1},\xi_{2})\right]\,d\xi_{1}\,d\xi_{2}\>, (3)

where the integral is over the lens plane, ff is the observed GW frequency, (1+zL)​f(1+z_{\scriptscriptstyle\text{L}})f is the blueshifted frequency of the GW on the lens plane (zLz_{\scriptscriptstyle\text{L}} is the redshift of the lens), and the distances DOSD_{\scriptscriptstyle\text{OS}}, DOLD_{\scriptscriptstyle\text{OL}}, and DLSD_{\scriptscriptstyle\text{LS}} are the distances between the observer (us) and the GW source, between the observer and the gravitational lensing object, and between the lensing object and the source, respectively [279]. In a cosmological setting, these are angular diameter distances [180]. The geometric optics limit corresponds to Fermat’s principle, in which the geodesic paths taken by GW are those passing through the lens plane at extrema of this two-dimensional time delay field T⁡(ξ1,ξ2)T(\xi_{1},\xi_{2}), which may be local minima, which produce Type I images, local maxima, which produce Type III images, or saddle points, which produce Type II images [279]. Equation (3) is evaluated in this high-frequency limit by use of the stationary phase approximation to obtain

Fj​(±|f|)=μj​exp⁡(∓2​π​i​|f|​tj±i​π​nj),F_{j}(\pm|f|)=\sqrt{\mu_{j}}\exp\left(\mp 2\pi i|f|t_{j}\pm i\pi n_{j}\right)\>, (4)

where μj\sqrt{\mu_{j}} and tjt_{j} are the magnification amplitude and observed time delay of image jj, and njn_{j} is 0, 1/2, or 1 for Type I, Type II, and Type III images, respectively. Therefore, such images are magnified or demagnified by a factor that is positive for Type I images and negative for Type III images, while the gravitational waveform of Type II images is additionally distorted, appearing as the Hilbert transform of the original waveform [121, 141]. For GW transients, the images are a set of repeated signals from the same event observed at different times, the delays determined by the differences in the time delay field on the lens plane of the different images. These delays are typically minutes to months for galaxy lenses [206, 238, 241] and up to years for galaxy cluster lenses [287, 286, 264, 272]. The images also appear at different points on the sky, with arcminute-scale separation, but GW detectors have insufficient sky-localization capabilities to distinguish them in this way. When gravitational lensing can be described in this geometric optics limit, it is referred to as strong lensing.

However, when the wavelength of the GW is comparable to the Schwarzschild radius of the gravitational lens, the geometric optics limit of Fermat’s principle is no longer valid, and the Fresnel–Kirchhoff diffraction formula of Equation (3) must be used to determine the complex-valued and frequency-dependent magnification factor. Such lensing effects can result from objects having masses up to ​105 M⊙{10}^{5}\text{\,}\mathit{M_{\odot}} and searches can be done in a modeled [334, e.g.,] or phenomenological [210] way.

Searches for Gravitational-lensing Signatures in GW Signals

In the companion paper Abac et al. [8], we present searches for gravitational lensing signatures in GWTC-5.0. Such signatures sought include multiple images from strong lensing, individual Type II strongly lensed images, and waveform distortions induced by point-mass lensing.

V.1.4 GW Polarization and Propagation in Alternative Theories of Gravity

In GR, plane GW perturbations to flat spacetime propagate at the speed of light and contain two transverse polarizations. However, in modified theories of gravity extending beyond GR, additional polarizations may be present, including two transverse-longitudinal spin-1 vector modes, a transverse spin-0 scalar mode, and a longitudinal spin-0 scalar mode [135, 136, 329]. With multiple detectors, it is possible to test for such additional polarizations [280, 281]. A linear combination of strain data from three detectors, often called the null stream, can be formed in which any GW signal from a known sky location and containing only plus- and cross-polarizations is canceled [168, 197, 294, 118, 333]. Any residual GW signal found in such a null space would provide evidence for the presence of vector or scalar non-GR polarizations.

In addition, in alternative Lorentz invariance violating theories of gravity or in which the graviton is massive, GW are dispersive. Certain theories of dark energy also result in dispersive GW propagation [127, 82, 173]. The GW dispersion relation between the frequency ff and the wavelength λ\lambda (one where they are not inversely proportional) leads to phase speeds and/or group speeds that differ from the speed of light. Such propagation effects can be measured for a known waveform by the anomalous arrival times of different frequency components. A common parameterized dispersion relationship is motivated by a modified energy–momentum relationship for the graviton of the form [230]

E2=(p​c)2+Aα​(p​c)α,E^{2}=(pc)^{2}+A_{\alpha}(pc)^{\alpha}\>, (5)

where AαA_{\alpha} is a GR-violating parameter having dimensions of (energy)2−α\text{(energy)}^{2-\alpha}. For de Broglie waves, E=2​π​ℏ​fE=2\pi\hbar f and p=2​π​ℏ/λp=2\pi\hbar/\lambda, where 2​π​ℏ2\pi\hbar is the Planck constant. Such a modified energy–momentum relation leads to a dispersion relation in which the phase velocity vpv_{\mathrm{p}} is given by

(vpc)2=1+Aα​(2​π​ℏ​cλ)α−2,\left(\frac{v_{\mathrm{p}}}{c}\right)^{2}=1+A_{\alpha}\left(\frac{2\pi\hbar c}{\lambda}\right)^{\alpha-2}\>, (6)

where the phase velocity is related to the frequency and the wavelength of the GW, vp=λ​fv_{\mathrm{p}}=\lambda f. The group velocity, vg=vp−d​vp/d​ln⁡λv_{\mathrm{g}}=v_{\mathrm{p}}-dv_{\mathrm{p}}/d\ln\lambda, determines the difference in arrival times of different frequency components of the GW after propagation from its source to the observer. For small deviations from GR (vp≈cv_{\mathrm{p}}\approx c), the group velocity is frequency dependent with

vg−cc≈12​(α−1)​Aα​(2​π​ℏ​f)α−2.\frac{v_{\mathrm{g}}-c}{c}\approx\frac{1}{2}(\alpha-1)A_{\alpha}(2\pi\hbar f)^{\alpha-2}\>. (7)

Special cases include (i) a graviton of mass mg≠0m_{g}\neq 0 for which α=0\alpha=0, A0=mg2​c4A_{0}=m_{g}^{2}c^{4}, and

vg−cc≈−12​(λg​fc)−2,\frac{v_{\mathrm{g}}-c}{c}\approx-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\lambda_{g}f}{c}\right)^{-2}\>, (8)

where λg=2​π​ℏ/(mg​c)\lambda_{g}=2\pi\hbar/(m_{g}c) is the Compton wavelength of the graviton, and (ii) the case in which GW are nondispersive but propagate at a speed different from the speed of light for which α=2\alpha=2 and

vg=c​1+A2.v_{\mathrm{g}}=c\sqrt{1+A_{2}}\>. (9)

Stringent bounds on the latter are provided by the close temporal association of the BNS signal GW170817 and the gamma-ray burst GRB 170817A (the gamma rays arriving less than 2 s2\text{\,}\mathrm{s} after the BNS GW merger signal), resulting in |A2|≲10−14|A_{2}|\lesssim 10^{-14} [32].

The Einstein–Hilbert action of GR contains second derivatives of the spacetime metric [326, 232, 322, 105]. Standard Model extensions having modified actions containing third derivatives of the metric can produce CPT-violating terms33 3 Here, the CPT acronym indicates the symmetry of the Standard Model Lagrangian with respect to charge conjugation, spatial parity and time inversion. CPT-violating terms would violate this symmetry. in the gravitational field equations, which can produce birefringence effects in which different GW helicities propagate with different phase velocities [198, 199, 229, 169]. Other theories of gravitation also have GW with birefringent propagation [339]. Such birefringence leads to a frequency-dependent rotation of the GW polarization angle.

Both GW birefringence and the modified GW dispersion relation can potentially be anisotropic, where the magnitude of the observed effect depends on the direction to the source.

Tests of GR: GW Polarization and Propagation

In the companion paper Abac et al. [6], we test the GR prediction of the polarizations of GW by searching for evidence of vector- or scalar-polarization modes in observed GW signals. We also present tests of a modified dispersion relation using GW signals from CBC [16, and have presented tests of anisotropic birefringence in the past;], for which it is assumed that the GW near the source is described by GR to a good approximation, but the waveform is affected during propagation.

V.2 Compact Binary Coalescences

Binaries consisting of two BH (BBH systems), consisting of two NS (BNS systems), or in which one component is an NS and the other a BH (NSBH systems), have all been observed by the LVK [23, 27, 44]. The detectable signal produced by such systems arises from the late stage of orbital decay, driven by GW emission, and by the ensuing merger of the binary components and the settling of the resulting object (an NS or BH) to a final, stationary configuration [110].

Table 3 provides a list of parameters used to describe CBC.

V.2.1 Newtonian Inspiral

At early stages of the inspiral, when the magnitude of the difference in velocity vectors of the two components of the binary, vv, is much smaller than the speed of light, the orbit is determined approximately by Newtonian mechanics while the gravitational radiation is described by the quadrupole formula (139, corrected by 137, page 279). For a quasi-circular orbit that is inclined an angle ι\iota relative to the direction to an observer, h+h_{+} and h×h_{\times} are sinusoidal and are 90​° out of phase,

h+\displaystyle h_{+} =−2​(1+cos2⁡ι)​G​M​ηc2​r​(vc)2​cos⁡2​ϕ\displaystyle=-2(1+\cos^{2}\iota)\frac{GM\eta}{c^{2}r}\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{2}\cos 2\phi (10a)
and
h×\displaystyle h_{\times} =−4​cos⁡ι​G​M​ηc2​r​(vc)2​sin⁡2​ϕ,\displaystyle=-4\cos\iota\frac{GM\eta}{c^{2}r}\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{2}\sin 2\phi\>, (10b)

where rr is the distance between the source and the observer, M=m1+m2M=m_{1}+m_{2} is the total mass of the system, η=m1​m2/M2\eta=m_{1}m_{2}/M^{2} is the symmetric mass ratio, M​ηM\eta is the reduced mass of the system, and ϕ\phi is the orbital phase relative to the ascending node [248, 302, 151, 330]. The inclination angle ι\iota as well as other orbital elements and their relation with the GW are illustrated in Figure 5. When ι=0\iota=0 or ι=π\iota=\pi (face on and face off respectively), the amplitudes of the sinusoidal functions h+h_{+} and h×h_{\times} are equal and the GW is circularly polarized; when ι=π/2\iota=\pi/2 (edge on), h×=0h_{\times}=0, and the GW is linearly polarized.

The GW luminosity of such a system, i.e., the power in gravitational radiation, is

E˙GW=325​c5G​η2​(vc)10.\dot{E}_{\mathrm{GW}}=\frac{32}{5}\frac{c^{5}}{G}\eta^{2}\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{10}. (11)

This radiation gives rise to a secular orbital decay. Since the (Newtonian) energy of the bound system is Eorb=−(1/2)​η​M​v2E_{\mathrm{orb}}=-(1/2)\eta Mv^{2}, and equating E˙GW=−E˙orb\dot{E}_{\mathrm{GW}}=-\dot{E}_{\mathrm{orb}}, we deduce that the period of the orbit, P=2​π​G​M/v3P=2\pi GM/v^{3} by Kepler’s third law, evolves according to

P˙=−192​π5​η​(vc)5.\dot{P}=-\frac{192\pi}{5}\eta\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{5}. (12)

At fixed orbital period (or orbital frequency), the orbital velocity is proportional to the cube root of the total mass, v∝M1/3v\propto M^{1/3}. It can be seen, then, that h+,h×∝η​M5/3h_{+},h_{\times}\propto\eta M^{5/3}, E˙GW∝(η​M5/3)2\dot{E}_{\text{GW}}\propto(\eta M^{5/3})^{2}, Eorb∝η​M5/3E_{\mathrm{orb}}\propto\eta M^{5/3} and P˙∝η​M5/3\dot{P}\propto\eta M^{5/3}. At the Newtonian level of approximation, a single combination of the component masses,

ℳ=η3/5​M=(m1​m2)3/5(m1+m2)1/5,\mathcal{M}=\eta^{3/5}M=\frac{(m_{1}m_{2})^{3/5}}{(m_{1}+m_{2})^{1/5}}\>, (13)

known as the chirp mass, solely determines both the amplitude of a GW at fixed orbital frequency and its frequency evolution [187, 120, 151]. This chirp mass is normally the most accurately measured mass parameter for low-mass systems in which most of the signal observed arises from the pre-merger phase.

V.2.2 PN Inspiral and Other Effects

Additional terms in the GW amplitude and frequency evolution appear at higher orders in v/cv/c in a PN (PN) expansion in the equations of motion and in the gravitational emission [90]. At the Newtonian order, the frequency of the GW is twice the frequency of the orbital motion, f=2​forb=2/Pf=2f_{\mathrm{orb}}=2/P, and

v3=π​G​M​f.v^{3}=\pi GMf\>. (14)

At O⁡(v/c)O(v/c) beyond this, additional components to the GW at frequencies at one and three times the orbital frequency arise from current quadrupole and mass octupole radiation, and other components occur at O⁡(v2/c2)O(v^{2}/c^{2}) beyond Newtonian order from current octupole and mass hexadecapole radiation [301]; the amplitudes of these higher-order multipole moments of radiation are proportional to a different combination of component masses [193]. The frequency evolution also gains additional terms at O⁡(v2/c2)O(v^{2}/c^{2}) beyond the leading-order Newtonian term, again having a different dependence on the component masses from the leading Newtonian order [321].

Spin effects from rotating binary components also appear in PN corrections to the quadrupole waveform due to O⁡(v3/c3)O(v^{3}/c^{3}) spin–orbit and O⁡(v4/c4)O(v^{4}/c^{4}) spin–spin effects [194] and to precession of the orbital plane if the spin angular momentum vectors of the bodies are not aligned (or antialigned) with the orbital angular momentum vector [76]. The binary precesses around the (approximately) constant direction of total angular momentum 𝑱{\boldsymbol{J}}, which is the vector sum of the orbital angular momentum and the spin angular momenta of the two bodies (𝑱=𝑳PN+𝑺1+𝑺2{\boldsymbol{J}}={\boldsymbol{L}}_{\text{PN}}+{\boldsymbol{S}}_{1}+{\boldsymbol{S}}_{2}, with 𝑳PN\boldsymbol{L}_{\text{PN}} the Newtonian orbital angular momentum 𝑳\boldsymbol{L} with PN corrections). The source inclination angle θJ​N\theta_{JN}, the angle between 𝑱\boldsymbol{J} and the direction to Earth 𝑵\boldsymbol{N} (see Figure 5) is often reported instead of the orbital inclination angle ι\iota. The dimensionless effective inspiral spin parameter χeff\chi_{\mathrm{eff}}, defined as

χeff=cG​M​𝑳⋅(𝑺1/m1+𝑺2/m2)|𝑳|,\chi_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{c}{GM}\frac{\boldsymbol{L}\cdot({\boldsymbol{S}_{1}/m_{1}+\boldsymbol{S}_{2}/m_{2}})}{|\boldsymbol{L}|}, (15)

where 𝑺1\boldsymbol{S}_{1} and 𝑺2\boldsymbol{S}_{2} are the spins of the two binary components and 𝑳\boldsymbol{L} is the orbital angular momentum about the center of mass, is a convenient spin parameter that is conserved under the orbit-averaged precession equations of motion at O⁡(v4/c4)O(v^{4}/c^{4}) [123, 259, 67, 274, 192]. Whereas χeff\chi_{\mathrm{eff}} depends on the spin components aligned with the orbital angular momentum, a dimensionless effective precession spin parameter that depends on in-orbital-plane components of the spins,

χp=cG​m1​max⁡{|𝑳×𝑺1/m1||𝑳|,3​m1+4​m23​m2+4​m1​|𝑳×𝑺2/m2||𝑳|},\chi_{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{c}{Gm_{1}}\max\left\{\frac{|\boldsymbol{L}\times\boldsymbol{S}_{1}/m_{1}|}{|\boldsymbol{L}|},\frac{3m_{1}+4m_{2}}{3m_{2}+4m_{1}}\frac{|\boldsymbol{L}\times\boldsymbol{S}_{2}/m_{2}|}{|\boldsymbol{L}|}\right\}\>, (16)

captures the dominant precession effects [278].

Deformable binary components (NS but not BH) suffer an induced quadrupole deformation Qi​jQ_{ij} under an external tidal field ℰi​j{\mathcal{E}}_{ij}, where these quadrupole tensors are those appearing in a multipole expansion of the Newtonian potential centered on the body of mass mm as [303]

Φ⁡(𝒙)=−G​m|𝒙|−12​G​Qi​j​3​xi​xj−|𝒙|2​δi​j|𝒙|5+12​ℰi​j​xi​xj+⋯.\Phi(\boldsymbol{x})=-\frac{Gm}{|\boldsymbol{x}|}-\frac{1}{2}GQ_{ij}\frac{3x^{i}x^{j}-|\boldsymbol{x}|^{2}\delta^{ij}}{|\boldsymbol{x}|^{5}}+\frac{1}{2}{\mathcal{E}}_{ij}x^{i}x^{j}+\cdots\>. (17)

The dimensionless tidal deformability, Λ\Lambda, of a body of mass mm is defined in terms of the ratio of the induced deformation to the external tidal field as

G​Qi​j(G​m/c2)5=−Λ​ℰi​j,\frac{GQ_{ij}}{(Gm/c^{2})^{5}}=-\Lambda{\mathcal{E}}_{ij}\>, (18)

where BH have Λ=0\Lambda=0. Newtonian tidal interactions of deformable components appear as effective O⁡(v10/c10)O(v^{10}/c^{10}) corrections to the binding energy and GW luminosity [154]. At this order, the dimensionless combination of tidal parameters given by [149]

Λ~=1613​(m1+12​m2)​m14​Λ1+(m2+12​m1)​m24​Λ2(m1+m2)5\tilde{\Lambda}=\frac{16}{13}\frac{(m_{1}+12m_{2})m_{1}^{4}\Lambda_{1}+(m_{2}+12m_{1})m_{2}^{4}\Lambda_{2}}{(m_{1}+m_{2})^{5}} (19)

appears, where Λ1\Lambda_{1} and Λ2\Lambda_{2} are the dimensionless tidal deformabilities of the two bodies, and it is this parameter that is most measurable in the waveforms produced by binaries with deformable companions [254]. Spinning bodies experience quadrupole deformation of the form

Qi​j=diag⁡(−13​Q,−13​Q,23​Q),Q_{ij}=\mathrm{diag}\left(-\frac{1}{3}Q,-\frac{1}{3}Q,\frac{2}{3}Q\right)\>, (20)

where QQ is the spin-induced mass quadrupole moment scalar and the body spins about the third coordinate axis. The quadrupole deformations induced by an object’s spin result in Newtonian quadrupole–monopole effects as an effective O⁡(v4/c4)O(v^{4}/c^{4}) correction, the same order as the spin–spin coupling relativistic effects [253]. The size of the spin-induced deformation depends on the nature of the body, where the ratio of the quadrupole scalar to the square of the body’s spin magnitude is given by the dimensionless parameter κ\kappa as

Q=−κ​|𝑺|2m​c2,Q=-\kappa\frac{|\boldsymbol{S}|^{2}}{mc^{2}}\>, (21)

where mm is the mass of the body. For a BH, κ=1\kappa=1 [301].

Binaries detected by ground-based observatories are commonly assumed to have negligibly small orbital eccentricity remaining by the time the orbital period has decayed to the point that the GW frequencies have entered the high-frequency sensitivity band of the detectors. This decay in eccentricity happens because orbital eccentricity is efficiently reduced by GW emission during the orbital decay [247]. However, there are channels of compact binary formation that could result in nonnegligible orbital eccentricity being present even at the last stages of inspiral observed by ground-based detectors [220, e.g.,]. Moreover, the Kozai–Lidov resonance [319, 235] due to the hierarchical interaction of a binary with a third body, possibly in a crowded stellar environment [196, 170], can also play an important role by sustaining high levels of eccentricity and increasing the merger rate [311]. The leading-order effects of orbital eccentricity would appear at the Newtonian level [248]. Two additional parameters are needed to describe an eccentric binary system, the eccentricity ee and the argument of the periapsis ω\omega. Although these are well-defined for Newtonian two-body systems, there are different ways to generalize their definitions for relativistic systems, and there is not yet a settled convention for these parameters [282].

Tests of GR from CBC Inspiral

PN theory in GR predicts the relative amplitudes of subdominant modes of GW radiation [90], which depend on the binary’s masses and spins [77, e.g.,]. Thus, allowing for freedom in these amplitudes and checking whether they are consistent with those predicted by GR provides a consistency test of the agreement of the signal with the waveform model used to analyze it [258]. In a past companion paper [17], this test is carried out for BBH signals, considering deviations, δ​Aℓ​m\delta A_{\ell m}, in the amplitude of the (ℓ=2,m=±1)(\ell=2,m=\pm 1) or (ℓ=3,m=±3)(\ell=3,m=\pm 3) subdominant multipole moments relative to the dominant (ℓ=2,m=±2)(\ell=2,m=\pm 2) and other multipole moments.

The PN expansion of the orbital energy and GW energy loss makes a prediction of how the GW phase evolves with time as the orbit decays [90]. The PN formalism expresses this phase evolution with a set of coefficients in a series expansion of the GW phase in terms of powers (v/c)n−5(v/c)^{n-5} and (v/c)n−5​log⁡(v/c)(v/c)^{n-5}\log(v/c) for integer nn (with n=0n=0 for the leading-order Newtonian inspiral) that depend on the binary components’ masses and spins for point particles. Violations of GR can lead to differences in the values of the PN coefficients from those predicted by GR [337, 295, e.g.,], which could be observed in a GW signal [91, 92, 78, 231, 207]. In the companion paper Abac et al. [6], we present parameterized tests for such violations.

Effects arising from the finite size of the component masses of a binary include spin-induced multipole moments, most importantly their spin-induced quadrupole moments QQ, which also affect the orbital evolution. For a BH, there is a fixed relation between its spin-induced quadrupole moment and its mass and spin [253]. Deviations from this predicted value, as observed in the phase evolution of a GW signal, can be used to distinguish a BBH from a compact binary containing exotic, non-BH components. Some examples of exotic alternatives to BH, being compact objects capable of having masses greater than the maximum mass of an NS, include boson stars [189, 271], gravastars [225], fuzzballs [223], and firewalls [73]. Past companion papers [16, most recently] have presented such parameterized tests of the nature of the components of CBC.

V.2.3 Compact Binary Merger and Ringdown

The final stages of GW emission from CBC that result in a BH remnant can be modeled as a linear gravitational perturbation to a Kerr BH spacetime [256]. Remarkably, the partial differential equations for the outgoing GW content of such a perturbation decouple from the other gravitational modes, and those decoupled equations are separable into a radial equation, an angular equation, and an exponential function of time with a complex frequency [298, 299]. The separation results in a spectrum of complex eigenfrequencies of the GW perturbations to the BH spacetime indexed by integer degree ℓ\ell and order mm numbers, ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 and |m|≤ℓ|m|\leq\ell, and integer overtone nn with n≥1n\geq 1 [203, 87]. The angular eigenfunctions, which depend on ℓ\ell and mm, also depend on the dimensionless complex frequency and the dimensionless spin parameter of the remnant BH. The complex eigenfrequencies describe the spectrum of exponentially decaying sinusoidal GW quasi-normal modes that make up what is called the BH ringdown. GR therefore provides a prediction for the relationship between the frequency and the decay constant for the spectrum of such quasi-normal modes that depend solely on the mass and spin of the final BH, and thus the BH ringdown radiation can be used to test these predictions of GR.

Spanning the region between the portion of the waveform that can be computed by PN calculations at early time and the portion that can be computed by a superposition of quasi-normal modes at late time is what is known as the merger phase of the compact binary. Due to the nonperturbative nature of this phase, NR (NR) solutions to Einstein’s field equations are sought [204, 134]. Such solutions both interpolate these early and late phases and also provide the information about the quasi-normal mode amplitudes and phases excited as well as the mass and spin of the remnant BH [179, 175, 185].

When at least one component of the binary in the CBC is not a BH (i.e., an NS), the merger and ringdown phases might be considerably more complex owing to the presence of matter in the system. NR is typically required to compute the entire post-inspiral phase of the GW emitted from such systems [142, 202]. One important piece of such simulations is to determine whether disruption of an NS component occurs, particularly in the case of NSBH systems in which the NS might be swallowed whole by the BH (typical for high-mass and low-spin BH) or might be tidally disrupted by the BH (typical for low-mass or high-spin BH). Such NS disruption would be expected to produce electromagnetic emission that could be observed by electromagnetic astronomical observatories. Guided by numerical simulations, one can estimate whether a system having particular parameters inferred from the inspiral phase will be electromagnetically bright and so a candidate for electromagnetic follow-up observations [156, 108, 86].

Depending on the masses of the initial components, the product of the merger of two NS might be another NS, a supramassive NS (a uniformly spinning NS that is more massive than the highest allowed mass for a nonspinning NS, which remains an NS until its angular momentum is dissipated, resulting in its collapse to a BH), a hypermassive NS (an NS more massive than would be allowed for any stationary, spinning configuration, but which is temporarily supported by differential rotation, and which will ultimately collapse to a BH), or there might be a direct collapse on a dynamical timescale to form a BH after the merger [84, 252]. Both the electromagnetic emission and GW emission from these different scenarios are expected to vary considerably [29].

Tests of GR from CBC Merger

NR simulations of BBH in GR provide predictions for the GW waveform spanning the inspiral, merger, and final ringdown phases of evolution. Tests for violations of GR can be performed by subtracting the best-fit GR waveform from the observed data and testing whether the remaining residual is consistent with detector noise or whether there is remaining signal present. Alternatively, since NR predicts how a final BH mass and spin are related to the initial BH masses and spins for a BBH CBC [179, 175, 185], a test of consistency between the initial orbital parameters and the final BH mass and spin can be performed. Here, the initial component BH masses and spins can be determined from the early inspiral phase of the GW signal, while the mass and the spin of the final BH are found from the late-time ringdown radiation. In practice, such a consistency test divides the GW signal into low- and high-frequency portions (below and above a given cutoff frequency) that are independently modeled with full inspiral–merger–ringdown waveforms [161, 162]. Companion paper Abac et al. [6] presents results from such a residual test and past companion papers [17, most recently] have also presented inspiral–merger–ringdown consistency tests.

In GR, a BH remnant produced by a CBC will rapidly settle to a stationary Kerr BH [191], uniquely characterized by its mass and spin [183, 106], through emission of ringdown radiation in a spectrum of quasi-normal modes, as described earlier. These quasi-normal modes have a discrete spectrum of complex-valued eigenfrequencies (the imaginary part of which determines the decay timescale), so a possible non-BH remnant [214, e.g.,], or modifications of the spectrum in alternative theories of GR [101, e.g.,], can be tested by looking for deviations in the observed ringdown radiation from the anticipated spectrum of quasi-normal modes [88].

Furthermore, if the remnant object does not possess an event horizon, ingoing GW radiation can be reflected off of a surface or scattered off of an inner potential and reemerge as an echo signal observed within a few seconds after the merger [103, 104, 283]. The companion paper Abac et al. [6] presents tests of the nature of the remnant resulting from CBC through observed quasi-normal mode spectra. Past companion papers [18, most recently] have also presented searches for GW echoes.

The post-inspiral portion of a BBH signal can be phenomenologically modeled with various parameters that are fitted to NR simulations [255]. Past companion papers [16, most recently] have explored possible deviations of these parameters from their nominal values [227, 269].

V.2.4 Redshift and Cosmological Effects

\Acp

GW can be redshifted, just as electromagnetic waves are. These changes are caused by the Doppler effect due to relative motion of the emitter and the observer (often described in terms of peculiar velocities relative to the rest frame of the cosmological microwave background radiation), due to the expansion of space between the emitter and the observer, or due to gravitational redshift if the emitter and observer have different gravitational potentials. For sources beyond the nearby Universe (having redshifts ≳0.1\gtrsim 0.1), cosmological expansion is the dominant source of redshift [249].

The redshift is the fractional difference between the frequency of a wave at emission at its source fsrcf_{\text{src}}, and its observed frequency at a detector fdetf_{\text{det}}, z=(fsrc−fdet)/fdetz=(f_{\text{src}}-f_{\text{det}})/f_{\text{det}} [180]. Thus, the observed frequency of a wave is related to its emitted frequency by fdet=fsrc/(1+z)f_{\text{det}}=f_{\text{src}}/(1+z). Similarly, an interval in time in the source-frame d​tsrcdt_{\text{src}} is related to an observed interval in time by a detector d​tdetdt_{\text{det}} by d​tdet=(1+z)​d​tsrcdt_{\text{det}}=(1+z)dt_{\text{src}}. Equations (10) and (12) are both parameterized in terms of the orbital velocity vv, which is related to the GW frequency ff in the dominant mode by Equation (14). At a fixed moment in a GW waveform, where the binary has some instantaneous value of vv, we have

v3=π​G​M​fsrc=π​G​M​(1+z)​fdet.v^{3}=\pi GMf_{\text{src}}=\pi GM(1+z)f_{\text{det}}. (22)

That is, a redshifted signal, observed at frequency fdetf_{\text{det}}, produced by a system with intrinsic mass MM has identical morphology to an unredshifted signal produced by a system with intrinsic mass (1+z)​M(1+z)M [201]. If the redshift is unknown, then the observable mass parameters are the various combinations of (1+z)​m1(1+z)m_{1} and (1+z)​m2(1+z)m_{2}, e.g., (1+z)​ℳ(1+z)\mathcal{M} and (1+z)​M(1+z)M. These mass parameters with the 1+z1+z scale factor are referred to as detector-frame masses, m1det=(1+z)​m1m_{1}^{\text{det}}=(1+z)m_{1}, m2det=(1+z)​m2m_{2}^{\text{det}}=(1+z)m_{2}, Mdet=(1+z)​MM^{\text{det}}=(1+z)M, and ℳdet=(1+z)​ℳ\mathcal{M}^{\text{det}}=(1+z)\mathcal{M}. PN corrections to the waveform preserve this degeneracy for point particles (and BH). However, for NS, a functional relationship between the mass of an NS and its tidal deformability means that a measurement of Λ~\tilde{\Lambda} can break the degeneracy between mass and redshift, allowing the two to be independently measured [228].

The amplitudes of h+h_{+} and h×h_{\times} given in Equation (10) also depend on the total mass through the factor M/rM/r. If the factor (1+z)​M(1+z)M is determinable from the rate of decay of the orbital period, Equation (12), then the amplitude factor can be written as [(1+z)​M]/[(1+z)​r][(1+z)M]/[(1+z)r], suggesting that the measurable amplitude distance parameter is (1+z)​r(1+z)r.

The parameter rr that appears in inverse proportion to the GW amplitude in Equation (10) represents the areal radius, i.e., spheres centered on the GW source have area 4​π​r24\pi r^{2}. Within a cosmological setting, this parameter is the transverse comoving distance DMD_{\text{M}} [180]. Then, if the redshift is entirely due to the cosmological expansion of spacetime, the combination (1+z)​DM(1+z)D_{\text{M}} is equal to the luminosity distance of the source, and this becomes the observable distance parameter from the GW amplitude. In this sense, then, given a known cosmology (i.e., the values of the Hubble constant, matter density, and the spatial curvature), the functional relationship between luminosity distance and redshift allows the determination of the latter from the former, and the intrinsic masses, e.g., MM, can then be deduced from the observed mass–redshift combined parameters, e.g., Mdet=(1+z)​MM^{\text{det}}=(1+z)M. However, if other redshift effects are present, e.g., due to peculiar motion of the source or the observer relative to the Hubble flow, the combination (1+z)​DM(1+z)D_{\text{M}} is no longer equal to the luminosity distance.

Nevertheless, when reporting the parameters of a CBC, we normally assume that cosmological expansion is the only significant source of redshift, and so the observed amplitude parameter (1+z)​DM(1+z)D_{\text{M}} is referred to as luminosity distance DLD_{\mathrm{L}}, while a dimensionful intrinsic mass parameter such as the primary mass m1m_{1} is derived from observed detector-frame mass parameters as m1=m1det/[1+z⁡(DL)]m_{1}=m_{1}^{\text{det}}/[1+z(D_{\mathrm{L}})], where the relationship between the redshift and the luminosity distance, z⁡(DL)z(D_{\mathrm{L}}), is obtained by some standard cosmological model. The only case where this was not done was for GW170817, where the measured geocentric redshift to its host galaxy NGC 4993 was used [34]. The main uncertainty in the chirp mass of the system comes from the unknown peculiar velocity of the system relative to its host galaxy. Unless otherwise specified, the reference cosmology used to relate luminosity distance to redshift throughout the works is a ΛCDM model [246] corresponding to a spatially flat Friedman–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker spacetime [158, 157, 205, 265, 266, 267, 323, 326, 232] with Hubble constant H0=67.9 km s−1 Mpc−1H_{0}=$67.9\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}\text{\,}{\mathrm{Mpc}}^{-1}$, matter density parameter Ωm=0.3065\Omega_{\text{m}}=$0.3065$, and cosmological constant density parameter ΩΛ=1−Ωm=0.6935\Omega_{\Lambda}=1-\Omega_{\text{m}}=$0.6935$ [65, column TT+lowP+lensing+ext of Table 4].

Constraints on Cosmic Expansion from GW Observations

If the redshift of a GW source can be determined independently of its distance, then a distance–redshift relationship can be obtained and used to infer cosmological parameters [280, 201]. Here the CBC is called a standard siren (akin to the standard candles such as Cepheid variables and Type Ia supernovae used to measure distances to their galaxy hosts), where the luminosity distance of the CBC is inferred from the amplitude of the GW [181]. The most direct method of determining the redshift of a GW source is if there is an electromagnetic counterpart in which spectroscopic measurements of the redshift of its host galaxy can be made [201, 181, 122, 111]. This method is known as the bright sirens method. For example, the BNS coalescence GW170817 [27] was associated with the optical kilonova AT 2017gfo in the galaxy NGC 4993 [28], which allowed for a measurement of the maximum a posteriori value of the Hubble constant with 68.3 %68.3\text{\,}\mathrm{\char 37\relax} CL (CL) highest density interval 69−8+1769^{+17}_{-8} km s−1 Mpc−1\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}\text{\,}{\mathrm{Mpc}}^{-1} [39].

If no electromagnetic counterpart to a GW is observed, various methods are available to deduce the associated redshift (BBH are not normally expected to produce any electromagnetic radiation, unless there is matter present in their environment). One such method, the galaxy catalog method, also called the dark siren method, is to obtain statistical association of GW sources with potential host galaxies observed in surveys [280, 215]. This is usually done simultaneously with information obtained from another method, the spectral siren method. In the spectral siren method, a known feature in the mass distribution of the population of CBC is used to statistically infer the redshift of a number of sources at a given distance by how the observed detector-frame mass distribution is shifted with respect to the local (zero-redshift) distribution [113, 297, 146, 222]. Finally, future observations of BNS mergers may be capable of directly inferring the redshift of the source from the GW signal alone through measurements of the NS tidal deformations [228, 109].

The companion paper Abac et al. [7] reports on constraints on the cosmic expansion history based on combined CBC bright and dark sirens, including both the galaxy catalog method and the spectral siren approach. If GW propagate through cosmological backgrounds differently from electromagnetic waves in a manner that produces a different distance–amplitude relation, the modified propagation effects can be observed using standard siren methods [85]. The companion paper Abac et al. [7] also reports on constraints on such effects of modified GW propagation.

V.2.5 Populations of compact binaries

With a multitude of observed CBC, one can infer the underlying population of these sources. In doing so, one needs to account for the detector selection effects, e.g., the fact that events that are farther away are less likely to be detected as compared to events that are nearby. One key element of the population that can be measured is the local merger rate density ℛ\mathcal{R}, representing the number of CBC occurring per unit time per unit volume in the local Universe [250, 195, 96, 89, 147, 26], or its evolution with cosmic redshift ℛ⁡(z)\mathcal{R}(z), which is the number of coalescences per unit source-frame time per unit comoving volume at a cosmological redshift of zz [153]. Another is the population distribution of masses and spins of merging compact binaries, p⁡(m1,m2,𝑺1,𝑺2)p({m_{1},m_{2},{\boldsymbol{S}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{S}}_{2}}), which might also evolve over cosmic history, p⁡(m1,m2,𝑺1,𝑺2|z)p({m_{1},m_{2},{\boldsymbol{S}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{S}}_{2}}|{z}). The measurement uncertainty in single-event parameters and the total number of detected events dictate the measurability of features in the population. These inferences are important in understanding the underlying astrophysical formation channels of compact binaries [293, 148, 338, 219, 115, e.g.,].

Inference of the Population of CBC

In the companion paper Abac et al. [5], we present measurements of the local rate of BNS, NSBH, and BBH mergers, inference of the evolution of the CBC rate over cosmological time, and inference of the distribution of masses and spins of CBC.

VI Synopsis

This paper serves as an introduction to the collection of papers accompanying the LVK’s GWTC-5.0. We have provided an overview of the GW detectors and observing runs of the LVK network and of the observed GW from CBC. The primary sequels to this introduction are a description of the methods used to perform searches for GW in LVK data and to characterize source properties of identified signals [3] and a summary of the main observations of GWTC-5.0, highlighting new CBC candidates from O4b and their estimated masses and spins [4]. Other companion papers presenting science results from the analysis of the GWTC-5.0 candidates are described in Section I. GWTC provides a prodigious census of over 300300 merging binary systems spanning two orders of magnitude in mass from ∼1 M⊙\sim 1\text{\,}\mathit{M_{\odot}} NS to remnant BH exceeding 100 M⊙100\text{\,}\mathit{M_{\odot}}. Study of these observations will provide new insight into the nature of these objects, their population distribution, and their formation channels. These GW observations allow for sensitive tests of GR and provide information about the cosmological expansion history.

Appendix A Acronyms and glossary

This is a reference of frequently used terms and acronyms.

A+

A+ refers to a configuration of LIGO following a series of upgrades, some in advance of O4 (such as the addition of a new 300 m300\text{\,}\mathrm{m} filter cavity for frequency-dependent vacuum squeezing), and some planned in advance of O5, such as installation of new optics with lower noise and loss [35, 117].

Asharp

Asharp (A-sharp) is a proposed upgrade of the A+ interferometers anticipated on a post-O5 timeline. The baseline Asharp design is a room-temperature 1 µ​m1\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} laser wavelength interferometer upgrade with larger test masses having coatings with lower thermal noise, higher laser power, and increased levels of vacuum squeezing [159].

AdV

AdV refers to an upgraded Virgo detector [57] with an advanced interferometer. Virgo operated with the AdV configuration during O2 and O3.

AdV+

AdV+ is an upgrade to the AdV detector to take place in two phases: the first phase for operation during O4, and the second phase for operation during O5.

aLIGO

aLIGO refers to an upgraded LIGO configuration with advanced interferometers installed at both LHO and LLO. LIGO operated with the aLIGO configuration during O1, O2, O3, and O4 [1].

BBH

Binary black hole. A binary system where both components are BH.

BH

BH.

BHNS

Black hole–neutron star specifically refers to systems in which the BH formed before the NS. See also NSBH.

bKAGRA

bKAGRA is a configuration with a cryogenic resonant side-band extraction interferometer. As a preliminary step, the bKAGRA Phase-1 run from April 28 to May 6, 2018, operated a 3-km Michelson interferometer with sapphire test masses and full suspension systems, cooling one mass to cryogenic temperature, and marked the first cryogenic operation using full suspensions. [69].

BNS

Binary neutron star. A binary system where both components are NS.

CBC

CBC. The gravitational-radiation-driven orbital decay resulting in merger of a binary system made of two compact objects (NS or BH).

CI

CI. See CL.

CL

CL. Given a n=1n=1 univariate or nn-dimensional multivariate random variable 𝒙\boldsymbol{x} having PDF (PDF) p⁡(𝒙)p({\boldsymbol{x}}) and a nn-dimensional region RαnR^{n}_{\alpha}, then the CL α\alpha of the region RαnR^{n}_{\alpha} is the probability of 𝒙\boldsymbol{x} lying in RαnR^{n}_{\alpha}, α=P⁡(𝒙∈Rαn)=∫Rαnp⁡(𝒙)​dn​x\alpha=P({\boldsymbol{x}}\in R^{n}_{\alpha})=\int_{R^{n}_{\alpha}}p({\boldsymbol{x}})\,d^{n}x. The region RαnR^{n}_{\alpha} is then known as a 100​α%100\alpha\% CL credible region, with special cases: credible interval (CI) if n=1n=1, credible area if n=2n=2, or credible volume if n=3n=3. When n>1n>1 we normally take RαnR^{n}_{\alpha} to be the region having the smallest volume that has CL α\alpha (the highest-density region). When n=1n=1 (CI), Rα1R^{1}_{\alpha} is normally chosen to be an equal-tailed interval (also known as a symmetric interval), from the α/2\alpha/2 quantile to the 1−α/21-\alpha/2 quantile, but sometimes the smallest highest-density interval is used instead.

EOS

EOS of an NS. For cold NS (having temperature below the Fermi temperature), the EOS (EOS) is of a barotropic fluid, a relationship between the energy density of the fluid and its pressure.

FAR

FAR. Often used as a detection threshold, the probability of any one or more of a sequence of statistical tests performed over a duration TT erroneously rejecting a null hypothesis is 1−exp(−T×FAR)1-\exp(-T\times\text{FAR}). FAR therefore has dimensions of time−1. When interpreted as a measure of a detection significance of a candidate detection, this is the rate at which noise alone would produce more significant candidates.

GEO

The GEO is a British–German   -shaped interferometric GW detector with 600 m600\text{\,}\mathrm{m} arms located near Hannover, Germany [331].

GR

GR. Einstein’s theory of gravitation.

GW

GW. See Sections I and V.1.

GWOSC

The GWOSC (formerly known as the LIGO open science center) was created to provide public access to GW data products [45]. The GWOSC online data and resources can be found at https://gwosc.org.

GWTC

The GWTC is the electronic catalog of GW transients observed by LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detectors produced by the LVK.

IFAR

IFAR. The reciprocal of FAR, IFAR=(FAR)−1\text{IFAR}=(\text{FAR})^{-1}, having dimensions of time. A larger IFAR implies a more significant candidate, while a larger FAR implies a less significant candidate.

IFO

IFO, a type of detector that uses laser interferometry to measure changes in the lengths of optical paths induced by GW.

IGWN

The IGWN is a self-governing consortium using ground-based GW interferometers to explore the fundamental physics of gravity and to observe the Universe. The observatory network includes the KAGRA, LHO, LLO, and Virgo detectors. In addition, the GEO detector serves as a technology test bed and operates in an astrowatch mode outside of other detectors’ observing periods.

iKAGRA

iKAGRA is a configuration of the KAGRA detector as a simple Michelson interferometer that consists of two end test masses and a beam splitter. The mirrors were fused silica mirrors at room temperature suspended by simplified systems. iKAGRA was operated from 2016 March 25 to 2016 March 31 and from 2016 April 11 to 2016 April 25 [68].

IMBH

Intermediate-mass black hole. A BH in the mass range ∼​102 M⊙ to ∼​105 M⊙\sim{10}^{2}\text{\,}\mathit{M_{\odot}}\sim{10}^{5}\text{\,}\mathit{M_{\odot}}.

IR1

IR1 is a six-month observing run planned to begin in late October or mid-November of 2026. See https://observing.docs.ligo.org/plan for updates on the LVK observing run plans.

KAGRA

KAGRA is a Japanese   -shaped interferometric GW detector with 3 km3\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{m} arms located underground at the Kamioka Mine in Japan [70].

KAGRA Collaboration

The KAGRA Collaboration is a group of more than 400 individuals that carries out science related to the KAGRA detectors and their observations.

LHO

The LHO, one of the two LIGO observatories, located in Hanford, Washington, is an   -shaped interferometric GW detector with 4 km4\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{m} arms.

LIGO

The LIGO consists of two widely spaced installations within the United States: one in Hanford, Washington (LHO), and the other in Livingston, Louisiana (LLO). LIGO is operated by the LIGO Laboratory, a consortium of the California Institute of Technology and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology funded by the US National Science Foundation. Furthermore, LIGO-India is a planned advanced GW observatory to be located in India as part of the worldwide network. LIGO-India is planned as a collaborative project between a consortium of Indian research institutions and the LIGO Laboratory in the USA, along with its international partners Australia, Germany and the UK.

LLO

The LLO, one of the two LIGO observatories, located in Livingston, Louisiana, is an   -shaped interferometric GW detector with 4 km4\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{m} arms.

LSC

The LSC, founded in 1997, is a group of more than 1000 scientists that carries out science related to the LIGO detectors and their observations.

LV

The LV. Prior to O3b, all observational results were published by the LV.

LVC

The LVC. The acronym LV is now preferred.

LVK

The LVK.

NS

NS.

NSBH

The general term for a neutron star–black hole binary: a binary system in which one component is an NS and the other is a BH. If used in distinction with BHNS, it refers to such systems in which the NS formed before the BH.

NR

NR, the use of numerical methods to solve relativistic field equations in curved spacetimes.

O1

The O1 began on 2015 September 12 and ended on 2016 January 19. The LHO and LLO detectors participated in this observing run.

O2

The O2 began on 2016 November 30 and ended on 2017 August 25, during which the LHO and the LLO detectors were operating. On 2017 August 1, the AdV detector joined the observing run, forming a three-detector network.

O3

The O3 began on 2019 April 1 and ended on 2020 March 27, during which the LHO, LLO, and Virgo detectors were operating. A commissioning break from 2019 October 1 to 2019 November 1 divided O3 into two parts, O3a and O3b. A subsequent short run, O3GK, from 2020 April 7 to 2020 April 21 with GEO and KAGRA observing, followed O3b.

O3a

The first, pre–commissioning-break part of O3, from 2019 April 1 until 2019 October 1, during which the LHO, LLO, and Virgo detectors were operating.

O3b

The second, post–commissioning-break part of O3, from 2019 November 1 until 2020 March 27, during which the LHO, LLO, and Virgo detectors were operating. O3b was planned to continue until 2020 April 30 but ended early owing to the COVID-19 pandemic.

O3GK

A short observing run after O3b from 2020 April 7 to 2020 April 21, during which the KAGRA and GEO detectors were observing. KAGRA had intended to join LIGO and Virgo at the end of O3, but the early end of O3b made this impossible.

O4

The O4 began on 2023 May 24 and ended on 2025 November 18. It is divided into parts, the first of which, O4a, covered the period from 2023 May 24 until a commissioning break from 2024 January 16 to 2024 April 10. During O4a, LHO and LLO were observing. Following the break, observing continued in O4b from 2024 April 10 until an end date of 2025 January 28, with LHO, LLO, and Virgo observing. It was decided to continue O4 observing in a third period O4c, beginning 2025 January 28 and lasting until 2025 November 18.

O4a

The O4a including data from 2023 May 24 until a commissioning break that began on 2024 January 16. During O4a, LHO and LLO were observing. During the first 4 weeks, KAGRA was also observing.

O4b

The O4b starting at the end of a commissioning break on 2024 April 10 and ending on 2025 January 28. During O4b, LHO, LLO, and Virgo were observing. It was decided to continue O4 observations with a third part, O4c, immediately following the end of O4b on 2025 January 28.

O4c

The O4c, extending the run beyond its intended end date through 2025 November 18. A commissioning break in O4c took place between 2025 April 1 and 2025 June 11.

O5

The O5 is the planned future observing run to follow O4.

PDF

PDF. Given an n=1n=1 univariate or nn-dimensional multivariate random variable 𝒙\boldsymbol{x}, the probability of 𝒙\boldsymbol{x} lying in an nn-dimensional region RnR^{n} is P⁡(𝒙∈Rn)=∫Rnp⁡(𝒙)​dn​xP({\boldsymbol{x}}\in R^{n})=\int_{R^{n}}p({\boldsymbol{x}})\,d^{n}x, where p⁡(𝒙)p({\boldsymbol{x}}) is the PDF.

PE

PE, the process of measuring the parameters that describe the source of a signal, e.g., the masses and spins of the binary components of a CBC, from the observational data.

PN

PN, a perturbative method of obtaining solutions to relativistic field equations based on slow-motion and weak-field expansion of the spacetime metric and the stress–energy source.

PSD

PSD. See Appendix B.

RF

RF, the radio-frequency range, from ∼1{\sim}1 to ∼150 MHz\sim 150\text{\,}\mathrm{MHz}

SNR

SNR. See Appendix B.

Virgo

The Virgo detector is a European   -shaped interferometric GW detector with 3 km3\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{m} arms located near Cascina, Italy (near Pisa).

VirgoNEXT

VirgoNEXT is a planned, post-O5, major upgrade of Virgo to fill the gap between the current phase, AdV+, and next-generation detectors.

Virgo Collaboration

The Virgo Collaboration manages the building, operation, and development of the Virgo detector.

Appendix B Conventions for data analysis

This appendix serves to define the data analysis conventions that will be used throughout the GWTC-5.0 companion papers. For a general introduction to data analysis we refer the reader to Abbott et al. [38] and references therein.

Time series a⁡(t)a(t) and frequency series a~​(t)\tilde{a}(t) are related to each other by our conventions for the Fourier transform

a~​(f)=∫−∞+∞a⁡(t)​exp⁡(−2​π​i​f​t)​𝑑t\tilde{a}(f)=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}a(t)\exp\left({-2\pi ift}\right)\,dt (23)

and its inverse transform

a⁡(t)=∫−∞+∞a~​(f)​exp⁡(+2​π​i​f​t)​𝑑f.a(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\tilde{a}(f)\exp\left({+2\pi ift}\right)\,df\>. (24)

With these conventions, the dimensions of a~\tilde{a} are [a~]=[a]×time[\tilde{a}]=[a]\times\text{time}.

Detector noise is often taken to be a stochastic Gaussian process. If n⁡(t)n(t) is a real-valued stochastic Gaussian process, then the one-sided PSD Sn​(f)S_{n}(f) is formally defined by

⟨n~∗​(f′)​n~​(f)⟩=12​Sn​(f)​δ​(f−f′),\langle\tilde{n}^{\ast}(f^{\prime})\tilde{n}(f)\rangle=\frac{1}{2}S_{n}(f)\delta(f-f^{\prime})\>, (25)

where ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle is a statistical ensemble average of realizations of n⁡(t)n(t) and n~∗\tilde{n}^{\ast} is the complex conjugate of n~\tilde{n}. The one-sided PSD is defined only for f≥0f\geq 0. With these conventions, the dimensions of SnS_{n} are [Sn]=[n]2×time[S_{n}]=[n]^{2}\times\text{time}. Real detector noise is neither entirely stationary nor Gaussian [38]. However, it is often sufficient to assume n⁡(t)n(t) is ergodic such that

Sn(f)=limT→∞2T|∫−T/2T/2n(t)exp(−2πift)dt|2.S_{n}(f)=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{2}{T}\left|\int_{-T/2}^{T/2}n(t)\exp\left({-2\pi ift}\right)\,dt\right|^{2}\>. (26)

The factor of two in the one-sided PSD ensures that the integrated power is

∫0∞Sn(f)df=limT→∞1T∫−T/2T/2n2(t)dt.\int_{0}^{\infty}S_{n}(f)\,df=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{-T/2}^{T/2}n^{2}(t)\,dt\>. (27)

The amplitude spectral density is defined to be the square root of the PSD, Sn1/2​(f)S_{n}^{1/2}(f).

We often use a detector-noise-weighted inner product [150] between two real-valued time series, a⁡(t)a(t) and b⁡(t)b(t), which is defined as

⟨a|b⟩\displaystyle\langle a|b\rangle =4​Re​∫0+∞a~∗​(f)​b~​(f)Sn​(f)​𝑑f\displaystyle=4\operatorname{Re}\int_{0}^{+\infty}\frac{\tilde{a}^{\ast}(f)\tilde{b}(f)}{S_{n}(f)}\,df (28a)
=∫−∞+∞a~∗​(f)​b~​(f)(1/2)​Sn​(|f|)​𝑑f,\displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\frac{\tilde{a}^{\ast}(f)\tilde{b}(f)}{(1/2)S_{n}(|f|)}\,df\>, (28b)

where Sn​(f)S_{n}(f) is the detector’s one-sided PSD for the readout noise from that detector. The second form, Equation (28b), is an appropriate generalization of the inner product for complex-valued time series.

Since GW detectors are insensitive at very low frequencies, the mean of the detector readout is arbitrary, and so we take the detector noise to have zero mean, ⟨n⁡(t)⟩=0\langle n(t)\rangle=0. Gaussian noise is then entirely characterized by its PSD and its distribution is given by the probability density

p⁡(n)=1W​exp⁡(−12​⟨n|n⟩),p({n})=\frac{1}{W}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\langle n|n\rangle\right)\>, (29)

where WW is a usually neglected normalizing constant, the path integral W=∫exp(−⟨n|n⟩/2)𝒟nW=\int\exp\left({-\langle n|n\rangle/2}\right)\,\mathcal{D}n.

Consider a template waveform u⁡(t)u(t) that is unit-normalized, ⟨u|u⟩=1\langle u|u\rangle=1, which is expected to match a hypothetical signal in detector data d⁡(t)d(t). The matched filter SNR is

ρmf=⟨u|d⟩.\rho_{\text{mf}}=\langle u|d\rangle\>. (30)

If data d⁡(t)=n⁡(t)+h⁡(t)d(t)=n(t)+h(t) contain Gaussian noise n⁡(t)n(t) plus a signal h⁡(t)h(t) that is perfectly matched by the template waveform, h⁡(t)∝u⁡(t)h(t)\propto u(t), then ρmf\rho_{\text{mf}} is a random variable having a normal distribution with unit variance and mean equal to the optimal SNR

ρopt=⟨h|h⟩.\rho_{\text{opt}}=\sqrt{\langle h|h\rangle}\>. (31)

The likelihood that detector data d⁡(t)d(t) contains a signal h⁡(t)h(t) is given by Equation (29) with n⁡(t)=d⁡(t)−h⁡(t)n(t)=d(t)-h(t),

p⁡(d|h)\displaystyle p({d}|{h}) =1W​exp⁡(−12​⟨d−h|d−h⟩)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{W}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\langle d-h|d-h\rangle\right) (32a)
=exp(−⟨d|d⟩/2)W​exp⁡(⟨h|d⟩−12​⟨h|h⟩)\displaystyle=\frac{\exp\left({-\langle d|d\rangle/2}\right)}{W}\exp\left(\langle h|d\rangle-\frac{1}{2}\langle h|h\rangle\right) (32b)
=p⁡(d|∅)​exp⁡(ρmf​ρopt−12​ρopt2),\displaystyle=p({d}|{\varnothing})\exp\left(\rho_{\text{mf}}\rho_{\text{opt}}-\frac{1}{2}\rho_{\text{opt}}^{2}\right)\>, (32c)

where ρmf\rho_{\text{mf}} is the matched filter SNR with unit-normalized template u⁡(t)∝h⁡(t)u(t)\propto h(t) and p(d|∅)=W−1exp(−⟨d|d⟩/2)p({d}|{\varnothing})=W^{-1}\exp\left({-\langle d|d\rangle/2}\right) is the likelihood under the no-signal hypothesis, d⁡(t)=n⁡(t)d(t)=n(t). The likelihood is viewed as a functional of h⁡(t)h(t) for a given realization of detector data d⁡(t)d(t). The second factor in Equation (32c) is the signal-to-noise likelihood ratio p⁡(d|h)/p⁡(d|∅)p({d}|{h})/p({d}|{\varnothing}). Note that the likelihood ratio is a monotonically increasing function of the matched filter SNR, and so ρmf\rho_{\text{mf}} is the uniformly most powerful test for a known signal in Gaussian detector noise [237]. If the amplitude of the signal is unknown, h⁡(t)=ρopt​u​(t)h(t)=\rho_{\text{opt}}u(t) with unknown ρopt\rho_{\text{opt}}, then the likelihood is maximized for ρopt=ρmf\rho_{\text{opt}}=\rho_{\text{mf}} and

maxρopt⁡p⁡(d|ρopt​u)=p⁡(d|∅)​exp⁡(12​ρmf2).\max_{\rho_{\text{opt}}}p({d}|{\rho_{\text{opt}}u})=p({d}|{\varnothing})\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho_{\text{mf}}^{2}\right)\>. (33)

For the Newtonian inspiral of Section V.2.1, the signal observed in a detector can be obtained in the frequency domain under the stationary phase approximation as [275, 120]

h~(f)=−5​π24G​ℳc3G​ℳc2​Deff(π​G​ℳ​fc3)−7/6exp(−iΨ(f)),\tilde{h}(f)=-\sqrt{\frac{5\pi}{24}}\frac{G\mathcal{M}}{c^{3}}\frac{G\mathcal{M}}{c^{2}D_{\text{eff}}}\left(\frac{\pi G\mathcal{M}f}{c^{3}}\right)^{-7/6}\exp\left({-i\Psi(f)}\right)\>, (34)

where Ψ⁡(f)\Psi(f) is the stationary phase function and

Deff=r[F+2(ϑ,φ,ψ)(12+12cos2ι)2+F×2(ϑ,φ,ψ)cos2ι]−1/2.D_{\text{eff}}=r\left[{F_{+}^{2}(\vartheta,\varphi,\psi)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\cos^{2}\iota\right)^{2}+F_{\times}^{2}(\vartheta,\varphi,\psi)\cos^{2}\iota}\right]^{-1/2}\>. (35)

is the effective distance [71], which is related to the distance to the binary rr by a factor that accounts for the orientation angles that describe the position of the source on the sky (ϑ,φ)(\vartheta,\varphi), its inclination ι\iota, and polarization angle ψ\psi. Since F+2+F×2≤1F_{+}^{2}+F_{\times}^{2}\leq 1 (with equality for a source on the zenith or nadir of an   -shaped interferometric detector), Deff≥rD_{\text{eff}}\geq r (with equality only if ι=0\iota=0 or ι=π\iota=\pi). The optimal SNR for such a signal is

ρopt=56​πG​ℳc2​Deff(π​G​ℳc3)−1/6∫0+∞f−7/3Sn​(f)​𝑑f.\rho_{\text{opt}}=\sqrt{\frac{5}{6\pi}}\frac{G\mathcal{M}}{c^{2}D_{\text{eff}}}\left(\frac{\pi G\mathcal{M}}{c^{3}}\right)^{-1/6}\sqrt{\int_{0}^{+\infty}\frac{f^{-7/3}}{S_{n}(f)}\,df}\>. (36)

The horizon distance DhorD_{\text{hor}} [71] of a source is the effective distance of a signal from such a source that has SNR ρopt\rho_{\text{opt}} equal to some detection threshold ρth\rho_{\text{th}}. Such sources would not be expected to be detected beyond the horizon distance, but not all nearer sources will be detected either. The sensitive volume [151, 112] is a measure of the effective volume of space in which randomly isotropically oriented and homogeneously distributed identical sources will produce signals in the detector with SNR ρopt\rho_{\text{opt}} greater than the threshold ρth\rho_{\text{th}},

V\displaystyle V =∫ρopt>ρthr2​sin⁡ϑ​sin⁡ι​𝑑r​𝑑ϑ​𝑑φ​𝑑ι​𝑑ψ∫sin⁡ι​𝑑ι​𝑑ψ\displaystyle=\frac{\int_{\rho_{\text{opt}}>\rho_{\text{th}}}r^{2}\,\sin\vartheta\,\sin\iota\,dr\,d\vartheta\,d\varphi\,d\iota\,d\psi}{\int\sin\iota\,d\iota\,d\psi} (37a)
=0.086 084 199 431 669 767 7×43​π​Dhor3.\displaystyle=$0.086\,084\,199\,431\,669\,767\,7$\times\frac{4}{3}\pi D_{\text{hor}}^{3}\>. (37b)

If the merger rate density is ℛ\mathcal{R} then the expected number of detections in time TT is ℛ​V​T{\mathcal{R}}VT. For a standard measure of detector sensitivity, a binary source of two 1.4 M⊙1.4\text{\,}\mathit{M_{\odot}} objects (ℳ=2−1/5×1.4 M⊙≈1.218 770 788 61 M⊙\mathcal{M}=2^{-1/5}\times$1.4\text{\,}\mathit{M_{\odot}}$\approx$1.218\,770\,788\,61\text{\,}\mathit{M_{\odot}}$) is considered and a threshold SNR of ρth=8\rho_{\text{th}}=8 is adopted [112]. The sensitive volume is converted into an equivalent spherical radius as V=(4​π/3)​R3V=(4\pi/3)R^{3} to obtain the BNS inspiral range R=Dhor/2.264 777 377 850 737 58R=D_{\text{hor}}/$2.264\,777\,377\,850\,737\,58$, Equation (1).

In practice a discrete Fourier transform is used rather than the continuous, and window choice will vary depending on the analysis goals and methodology. For more details on the spectrum and spectral density estimation and its use in GW data analysis, see https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-T1400010/public.

THIS APPENDIX WILL RECORD CHANGES MADE IN FUTURE UPDATES

GWTC-4.0
  • •

    Initial version of this document.

GWTC-5.0
  • •

    Updated catalog version throughout from GWTC-4.0 to GWTC-5.0.

  • •

    Extended observational coverage from the O4a (O4a) ending 2024 January 31 to the O4b (O4b) ending 2025 January 28.

  • •

    Added explicit references to newly published standalone O4b event papers: GW241011_233834, GW241110_124123, GW250114_082203 and GW240925_005809.

  • •

    Updated narrative and figures in Section 3 to extend cumulative observing timelines through O4b.

  • •

    Updates to Section 4 describing the detector evolution during O4b.

  • •

    Wording changes throughout for clarity and general improvements.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
